1380.title: Muslims as minorities
1380.hook: Muslims living as minorities, balancing faith and society
1380.howItsDone: Muslims living as minorities pray at work or school where space allows, look for halal food and Muslim burial, arrange leave for Friday prayer and Eid, and often open their mosques to neighbors; some follow scholars of the 'fiqh of minorities', others the classical schools directly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, young Muslims: the young men of the cave, and a Thursday night call carrying the faith forward.

Umm Salamah remembers it in her own words, kept in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad. A small group of Muslims, pressed hard in Mecca, crossed the sea to Abyssinia, a Christian kingdom ruled by a king known by his title, the Negus. In paraphrase, she says: we came to the land of Abyssinia, found there the best of neighbors, and could practice our religion in safety. Then envoys arrived from Mecca to have them sent back. The king called the Muslims in and asked them to speak for themselves. A minority, in a strange land, before a king of another faith.
screen: `ACROSS THE SEA TO ABYSSINIA.` → `THE BEST OF NEIGHBORS.` → `SPEAK FOR YOURSELVES.`

segments.voice: Ja'far, the Prophet's cousin, speaks for the group, and the king asks to hear something of their scripture. Ja'far recites from the opening of surah Maryam, about Mary and the birth of Jesus. Umm Salamah says the king wept until his beard was wet, and refused to hand them over. The minority was protected, in a scene of mutual respect. Muslims draw a principle from texts like this. A verse of the Qur'an, in paraphrase, says Allah does not forbid kindness and justice toward those who have not fought you over religion or driven you from your homes, and that Allah loves those who deal justly. Today, Muslims live as minorities in Europe and the Americas, in India and China, in Australia and across Africa. The questions are practical: where to pray at work, how to keep Friday prayer with a school schedule, finding halal food, Eid on a working day, a Muslim burial plot, being misunderstood in the news. Some scholars have built a whole field around these questions, called the fiqh of minorities. Others hold that the classical schools already have what is needed. Both are answering the same family's questions. Day to day, it looks like this. A Muslim nurse prays in a supply room on her break. A family explains Ramadan at a school meeting. A mosque opens its doors to the neighbors on Eid. Small, steady negotiations, made with a neighbor who may become, as Umm Salamah put it, the best of neighbors.
screen: `JA'FAR RECITES MARYAM; THE KING WEEPS.` · `KINDNESS AND JUSTICE TO NEIGHBORS.` · `PRAYER AT WORK, EID ON A WORKDAY.` · `SMALL, STEADY NEGOTIATIONS.`

segments.voice: Picture the small group arriving by sea in Abyssinia, carrying very little, not knowing who will welcome them. Then let the picture move to today: a family whose hijab is the only one at the grocery store, or the only family skipping lunch through Ramadan. If you pray, ask for good for them and for their neighbors, in your own words.
Muslims as minorities. From companions sheltered in Abyssinia to families today in Europe, the Americas, India, China and beyond, keeping faith among neighbors of other faiths. Today's word.
Your line: faith as a minority. Any neighbor can become the best of neighbors. Next, a new stretch: science and faith.

1381.title: Science and faith
1381.hook: Muslims who see the study of nature as reading Allah's signs
1381.howItsDone: Muslims point to verses that call the creation of the heavens and earth, night and day, and living things signs, ayat, and to the hadith on seeking knowledge; Muslim scientists and scholars today discuss how findings and faith fit together, with some looking for scientific wonders in the Qur'an and others cautioning against it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muslims as minorities: Abyssinia, a weeping king, and the best of neighbors.

"Will they not regard the camels, how they are created?" A line of the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words, from surah al-Ghashiyah. It doesn't argue. It points. And it keeps pointing: at the sky, how it is raised; at the mountains, how they are set; at the earth, how it is spread out. A scripture that stops in the middle of its message to say: look at the animal in front of you, and ask how it was made. So what happens when a person of faith picks up a microscope?
screen: `REGARD THE CAMELS.` → `THE SKY, THE MOUNTAINS, THE EARTH.` → `FAITH PICKS UP A MICROSCOPE.`

segments.voice: Start with a word that does double duty. In the Qur'an, ayah, plural ayat, is used for the verses of the scripture, and also for signs in the world. In surah Al 'Imran, in paraphrase, the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, are signs for people of understanding. Some Muslim writers put it simply: there are two books, the book revealed and the book of creation, and both are read for signs. Then an invitation to look. Beyond the camels, other verses point at rain, at bees, at the stages of a child in the womb, at the variety of languages and colors. In Ibn Majah, in paraphrase, the Prophet, peace be upon him, calls seeking knowledge a duty on every Muslim. The history has practical roots. Finding the qibla, the direction of prayer, and the times of the prayers took careful work with the sky. Tradition remembers scholars like Ibn al-Haytham, who studied how light and sight work, and Ibn Sina, who wrote on medicine. And the questions still open. Muslims today work across the sciences and discuss how faith and findings fit together. Some writers look for scientific wonders foretold in the Qur'an. Other scholars caution against this, because science revises itself, and they'd rather not tie a verse to a theory that may change. Some see no conflict to resolve at all: for them, studying a cell or a star is reading signs, and the reading itself is worship.
screen: `AYAH: A VERSE, AND A SIGN.` · `REGARD: CAMELS, RAIN, BEES, STARS.` · `THE QIBLA AND THE SKY.` · `OPEN QUESTIONS, HONESTLY KEPT.`

segments.voice: Notice the breath itself: air moving in, the chest rising, something in you taking what it needs without being asked. Then look at your own hand for a moment, the creases, the joints, the way it closes. If you pray, look at it the way the verse looks at the camel, and ask how it was made; if not, simply stay curious.
Science and faith. For Muslims who read the world as ayat, signs, studying nature is a way of reading the book of creation alongside the book revealed. Today's word.
Your line: science reads signs. Two books, and both are read for signs. See you tomorrow.

1382.title: Medicine and fasting
1382.hook: doctors and scholars on fasting with illness
1382.howItsDone: Muslims who are ill or traveling may leave the Ramadan fast and make up the days later; someone who cannot make them up may feed a person in need instead, and some consult both a doctor and a scholar before the month begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday: science and faith, and the study of the natural world as a way of reading signs. Your line was science reads signs. Today, the body doing the reading.

A clinic waiting room, a few weeks before Ramadan. A woman with diabetes holds a question she's carried all year: can I fast this time? Her doctor has an answer about blood sugar. Her imam has an answer about the law. What she wants is the two of them in the same room. And the Qur'an had already made space for her, in the very passage that commands the fast.
screen: `A QUESTION BEFORE RAMADAN.` → `A DOCTOR AND AN IMAM.` → `THE SAME PASSAGE.`

segments.voice: The verse that sets the fast carries its own exception. In Surah al-Baqarah, Pickthall's translation reads: "(for) him who is sick among you, or on a journey, (the same) number of other days." So the person who is ill and doesn't fast isn't breaking the rule. They're following it, and the days can be made up later. The same verse speaks of a ransom, feeding a person in need, which scholars apply to someone who can't make the days up at all, like a person with a lasting illness. The next verse gives the reason plainly: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." The hadith add a second thread. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, hears of a companion who fasts every day and prays all night, and tells him to ease off, because, in paraphrase, your body has a right over you. And in Sunan Abu Dawud he tells people to seek treatment, since Allah has not made a disease without making a remedy for it. Put those side by side: health is a trust. The body isn't simply yours to spend down; it's held on someone's behalf. So the question in the clinic isn't how tough are you. It's what will this do to you. Some scholars hold that the advice of a trustworthy doctor can settle it. They differ in the gray cases: how sick is sick enough, and whether an inhaler or an injection breaks the fast. That's why the doctor and the imam keep meeting.
screen: `THE EXCEPTION IS IN THE VERSE.` · `ALLAH DESIRETH FOR YOU EASE.` · `YOUR BODY HAS A RIGHT OVER YOU.` · `A DOCTOR AND A SCHOLAR, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Move your attention slowly up from your feet, noticing where you're tired, sore or tight, without fixing anything yet. Then ask one honest question: what have I been putting off, a checkup, a prescription, sleep, water, a talk with a doctor? If you pray, hold your body in mind as something entrusted to you; if you don't, simply hold the one thing you named.
Medicine and fasting. The fast of Ramadan carries its own exception for the sick, and the hadith tell people to seek a cure. Today's word.
Your line: health is a trust. Your body has a right over you, too. Until tomorrow.

1383.title: The environment
1383.hook: stewardship, no waste, water as sacred (6:141; 7:31)
1383.howItsDone: Muslim environmental groups and preachers often draw on the idea of humans as khalifah, stewards of the earth, and on the Qur'an's warnings against waste, and some mosques run tree-planting days and water-saving drives.

segments.voice: Yesterday: medicine and fasting, and the exception for the sick written into the very verse of the fast. Your line was health is a trust. Today the trust gets bigger than one body.

Who owns the river at the edge of town? The city that bills you for it? The farm upstream that pumps from it? The fish? A verse in the Qur'an doesn't settle the paperwork, but it changes the question. Before humans ever appear on the earth in the story, Allah tells the angels what a person will be. Not an owner. Something else.
screen: `WHO OWNS THE RIVER?` → `NOT AN OWNER.` → `SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: In Surah al-Baqarah, Pickthall translates the announcement like this: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." The Arabic word is khalifah. A viceroy rules, but in someone else's name. He holds land that isn't his, and he answers for it. So when Muslims speak about the environment, some of them begin here: humans as stewards, not owners. Second, no waste. In Surah al-An'am there's an almost lush verse about gardens, trellised and untrellised, date palms, olives, pomegranates, crops of every taste. Eat of the fruit, it says, pay what's due on the day of harvest, and don't be wasteful. The instruction comes back in Surah al-A'raf, beside every place of worship: "eat and drink, but be not prodigal. Lo! He loveth not the prodigals." Prodigal is an old word for someone who squanders. Even at a feast, there's a limit. Third, water. In Sunan Abu Dawud the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that Muslims are partners in three things: water, pasture and fire. Shared, not something one person can hoard while others go thirsty. And a line in Sahih al-Bukhari: if a Muslim plants a tree and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, it counts for him as charity. A bird. Put together, it's a quiet picture of the earth in this tradition: a trust on loan, with others at the table.
screen: `A VICEROY IN THE EARTH.` · `EAT AND DRINK, BUT BE NOT PRODIGAL.` · `PARTNERS IN WATER, PASTURE AND FIRE.` · `A TREE A BIRD EATS FROM IS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Walk back through yesterday and count the taps: the shower, the sink while you brushed, the kettle filled too full, the glass poured and left. Don't scold yourself; just see the water moving through your day, and pick one tap you could turn down. If you pray, keep the word viceroy in mind, holding something that isn't yours; if you don't, keep the picture of a shared river.
The environment. In the Qur'an's picture, the earth is held in trust by a viceroy, eaten from without waste, its water shared. Today's word.
Your line: stewards, not owners. The river was never only yours. Same time tomorrow.

1384.title: Green mosques
1384.hook: mosques going solar and saving water
1384.howItsDone: Some mosques install solar panels, fit water-saving taps at their wudu stations, or reuse washing water for gardens, and imams sometimes remind worshipers to use little water in wudu, following the Prophet's practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the environment, and Pickthall's word for the human role on the earth, viceroy. Your line was stewards, not owners. Today, that stewardship comes home to one building.

A row of solar panels on a mosque roof, tilted toward the sun. There's a neat fit in that. The same sun already runs the building's day: dawn, noon, afternoon, sunset, nightfall, every prayer time set by where it sits in the sky. Now it lights the lamps too. Downstairs, in the washing area, someone has fitted slower taps and piped the used water out to the garden.
screen: `PANELS ON THE ROOF.` → `THE SUN SETS THE PRAYER TIMES.` → `WATER TO THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Start with the word mosque. The Arabic is masjid, a place of sajdah, of bowing the forehead to the ground. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari widens it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, lists things given to him, and one is this: the earth has been made for me a masjid and a means of purification. The whole earth, a place to pray. So a mosque building is, in a sense, a small roofed piece of a much larger mosque, and caring for the ground outside isn't a different job from caring for the carpet inside. Second, water. Before prayer comes wudu: washing the hands, face and arms, wiping the head, washing the feet. Anas reports in al-Bukhari that the Prophet did his wudu with a mudd, a small measure of water, and bathed with just a few of those measures. A report in Sunan Ibn Majah, though its chain is debated, has him see a companion using a lot of water and ask what this excess is. Can there be excess in wudu? the companion asks. Yes, comes the answer, even if you are at a flowing river. Third, what that looks like now. Some mosques have put panels on their roofs, swapped open taps for slower ones at the wudu stations, or collected the washing water to irrigate gardens. Some plant trees in the courtyard for shade. None of this is a new law. It's an old instinct, the earth as a place of prayer and water used with care, meeting new tools.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a shared place where people gather, a mosque, a church, a temple, a hall, and walk through it slowly: the roof, the lights, the taps, the patch of ground out front. 1385.title: Halal food today
1385.hook: certification, supply chains, and the spirit of tayyib
1385.howItsDone: Muslims who keep halal often look for certification marks on meat and packaged food, check ingredient lists for things like pork gelatin or alcohol, and differ among themselves on questions such as stunning and the meat of the People of the Book.

segments.voice: Yesterday: green mosques, panels on the roof, slow taps at the wudu station, the whole earth a masjid. Your line was mosques going green. Today, from the roof to the plate.

A small logo in the corner of a package of chicken: a crescent, maybe, or Arabic letters, and an organization you've never heard of. Behind it is a whole chain: a farm, a slaughterhouse, a factory, a truck, a freezer, an inspector with a clipboard. A shopper glances at it for half a second. But the verse behind the logo has a second word, and it never fits on a label.
screen: `A SMALL LOGO.` → `A WHOLE CHAIN BEHIND IT.` → `THE WORD THAT DOESN'T FIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, from Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall: "O mankind! Eat of that which is lawful and wholesome in the earth." It's addressed to mankind, everyone at the table. And there are two words, not one. Lawful is halal: what's permitted. The Qur'an names what isn't, in Surah al-Ma'idah: carrion, blood, pork, and meat dedicated to anything other than Allah. Wholesome is tayyib: good, pure, pleasant. Halal is a line. Tayyib is a quality. Now the modern part. A certifying body checks the halal side: how the animal was slaughtered, whether a gelatin came from pork, whether a flavoring hides alcohol, whether the halal meat touched other meat on the line. That's real work. Certifiers and scholars don't all agree on the details, like whether an animal may be stunned before slaughter, or whether a machine may do the cutting. And some Muslims read another verse in al-Ma'idah, that the food of the People of the Book is lawful, as covering meat from Jews and Christians today, while others don't. Then the second word asks more than any stamp. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that Allah has prescribed excellence in everything, and that when you slaughter, you should do it well: sharpen the blade, and spare the animal suffering. Some Muslims hear tayyib in that, reaching back up the chain to how the animal lived and died; some now ask the same of the workers and the land. The logo can say halal. Only the whole chain can say good.
screen: `TWO WORDS: LAWFUL AND WHOLESOME.` · `HALAL IS A LINE. TAYYIB IS A QUALITY.` · `THE CERTIFIER CHECKS THE CHAIN.` · `SHARPEN THE BLADE, SPARE THE ANIMAL.`

segments.voice: Bring the last thing you ate to mind and trace it backward: who sold it, who carried it, who made it, where it grew or how it lived. You won't know most of the answers; just notice how long the chain is. If you pray, hold the two words together, lawful and wholesome, and give thanks as you usually do; if you don't, thank one link in the chain.
Halal food today. Food checked as lawful, from a certifier's stamp all the way back to the farm, with tayyib, wholesome and good, asking for more. Today's word.
Your line: lawful and good. Halal is the line; tayyib asks for more. I'll be here tomorrow.

1386.title: Islamic finance today
1386.hook: banks, mortgages and sukuk, and debates about them
1386.howItsDone: Muslims who avoid interest may use home financing from Islamic banks built on sale, lease or partnership, invest in sukuk, and consult scholars or Sharia boards on products, while some decide certain products are too close to conventional loans.

segments.voice: Yesterday: halal food, the logo on the package, and tayyib, the word that asks for more. Your line was lawful and good. Today, from the plate to the wallet.

A couple sits across a desk from a bank officer, holding a printout of a house they love. The numbers are fine. Then one of them asks a question the officer may not hear every day: is there interest in this? If there is, for them, the house may be off the table. That question has built a whole corner of modern banking, with its own mortgages, its own bonds, and its own arguments about whether it's done right.
screen: `A HOUSE THEY LOVE.` → `IS THERE INTEREST IN THIS?` → `A CORNER OF BANKING.`

segments.voice: The root is a line in Surah al-Baqarah. Some people said trade is just like usury, and the Qur'an answers, in Pickthall: "Allah permitteth trading and forbiddeth usury." The Arabic for usury is riba. In Sahih Muslim, Jabir reports that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who writes it down, and the two who witness it, and said they are all alike. So trade is open; earning money purely from lending money is not. How do you buy a house, then? Islamic banks offer a few shapes. In one, the bank buys the house and sells it to you at a known, fixed markup, paid over time. In another, the bank owns the house and you rent it until it's yours. In a third, you and the bank buy it together as partners, and month by month you buy out the bank's share while paying rent on the part it still owns. Bonds have a version too: sukuk, certificates of part-ownership in a real asset, where the return comes from that asset rather than from a loan. The debate is inside the tradition. Some scholars and critics say certain products are a conventional loan wearing an Arabic name: the monthly payment looks much the same. Others answer that the form is the substance: the bank really owns something and really carries risk, so it's a trade, not a loan. Muslims who care about this weigh both, and come down in different places.
screen: `ALLAH PERMITTETH TRADING.` · `THE BANK BUYS, THEN SELLS.` · `SUKUK: OWNING PART OF AN ASSET.` · `REAL TRADE, OR A NEW NAME?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one money arrangement in your life, a credit card, a car payment, rent, savings, and ask it three quiet questions: who owns what, who carries the risk, and where does the extra money come from? Just see it plainly. If you pray, hold your earnings in mind as something you'll be asked about; if you don't, simply hold the three questions.
Islamic finance today. Banks, mortgages and sukuk built around one verse: trade is permitted, riba is forbidden, and the arguments over where one ends and the other begins. Today's word.
Your line: finance without interest. Minorities, science, the body, the earth, the mosque, the plate, and now the wallet. Rest well.
